tagline: An alpine road through aspens, lake country and the Fremont River valley
intro: The Fishlake Scenic Byway climbs through mountain terrain, descends beside Fish Lake and continues toward Highway 72. The paved road is somewhat narrow. Utah designated the route a state scenic byway in 1990; the Utah Office of Tourism highlights its mountain scenery, high sagebrush flats and alpine lake. The 29.6-mile corridor includes SR-25 and county roads, continuing beyond the numbered state highway through Fishlake National Forest.

The lake road entered the state highway system in 1918 and received the number SR-25 in 1927. A federal aid project moved its western end south to Fish Lake Junction in 1935. The scenic designation later reached beyond the lake: in November 1992, the byway extended along Fremont River Road from Johnson Valley Reservoir to SR-72.

Start at Highway 24 and climb into Fishlake National Forest, four miles along Highway 25. Pando lies southwest of the lake; the route then follows the lake’s western shore. Beyond the resorts, meadowland and sagebrush flats lead toward Johnson Valley Reservoir. After crossing the Fremont River at Zedds Meadow, the road climbs steeply, then descends through drier country toward Highway 72. Near the lower river crossing, Mill Meadow Dam holds a small reservoir; Highway 72 lies three miles farther along.

moments.title: Pando
moments.text: Pando’s estimated 47,000 aspen stems look like individual trees, but they are genetically identical parts of one tree linked by a shared root system. That system spans 106 acres. Jerry Kemperman and Burton V. Barnes identified the clone in 1976; genetic analysis published in 2008 confirmed the earlier work. Its stems die individually and are replaced by new, genetically identical stems sent up from the roots. The age of the whole clone cannot be determined from tree rings. Friends of Pando and Fishlake National Forest work together to study and protect the tree, alongside the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources.

moments.title: Fish Lake
moments.text: Fish Lake occupies a graben, a valley dropped down along faults. The Mytoge Mountains rise sharply about 1,000 feet above its southeast shore, while Fish Lake Hightop Plateau bounds the northwest shore. The lake gives Fishlake National Forest its name. Geologist Clarence Dutton described its spruce and aspen groves in 1875. The north end has marsh and meadowland, beyond most of the resort development. Across the water, the long ridge of Mytoge Mountain forms the basin’s eastern boundary. Mounts Marvine and Hilgard stand to the north. The lake supports rainbow trout, splake, kokanee salmon and lake trout.

moments.title: Johnson Valley Reservoir
moments.text: The byway descends to Johnson Valley Reservoir, a square mile of water at the source of the Fremont River. Beyond the high point above the reservoir, Highway 25 crosses the river at Zedds Meadow. A steep climb leads into a long descent, with fewer trees and more open views. Farther down, pinyon and juniper occupy the lower elevations, while cottonwood and box elder grow along the river bottom. At the reservoir’s northern edge, the Gooseberry-Fremont Scenic Backway branches toward Salina Canyon, another road connection between the lake country and I-70.

practical: Fish Lake: Heavy snow may be a problem between Fish Lake and Highway 72. (checked 2026-10-11)
